en: Against brave Sarybai,
Who fixed his hatred on the people and slaughtered them,
He rode out alone,
To slay his foe if he could,
To wage a furious battle,
And deliver the multitude
From disaster.
Across peaks where mountains vanished,
Across bare projecting crags,
He made the whole universe tremble
As he thundered onward.
The land grew hazy with dust;
Külchoro, upheld by providence,
Was brave lion Seytek’s
Second in combat.
“There is no resisting fate,” he said,
And came to stand as his support,
Saying, “Your descendants remain behind you.”
It was as though he had made slaves
Of every living soul.
Into the nostrils of his nose
A mighty giant might have fit;
When the madman snorted,
It seemed he could suck in
The whole universe without letting it stir.
His body was tall as a plane tree;
The people, despairing of their precious lives,
Seemed unable to remain standing.
His hands and arms were like pillars;
It seemed he subdued the universe
And crushed every living creature.
His drooping eyelashes,
On the glowering infidel,
Were like the handle of a rawhide whip;
The accursed one’s appearance
Had always been just so.
When he moved, he was a glowing ember;
Among many marvels, none was so dreadful.
When the madman roared,
It seemed he seized the universe,
Plucked up every mortal hero,
And casually
Stuffed him into his sack.
By Almighty God’s power,
One of you is a warrior, another a hero,
And another is made of black earth.
Like beasts of countless kinds,
Living creatures are born in every form;
Such was Sarybai, the monster’s son.
When he saw Sarybai,
The gray wolf’s heart grew troubled;
His face was like a burning coal,
His nose like a vast ridge,
His eyes like tethering irons,
Able to overtake anyone he pursued.
His bristling mustache
Seemed sharp enough to pierce an army;
Such an upturned mustache—
No other human creature was like him.
The infidel’s thought,
The thought of this blazing warrior, was:
“If only I could crush the universe
And stuff it into a single sack;
Until the Day of Judgment,
If only I could take this entire world
As provisions for my journey;
If only I could destroy every living soul
And remain alone;
If only I could annihilate all existence
And bring slaughter upon the ages.”
Such was Sarybek’s nature.
Standing upright at his full height,
When the gray-wolf-born Semetey
Saw Sarybai,
His face changed.
When he saw the madman,
The false world seemed to constrict;
As he looked closely upon death,
The broad and tranquil world
Appeared narrow to his eyes.
You infidel fit only for the grave,
You end of the created age—
Who has ever seen such a warrior?
He alone was born into the world
As though intending to end the age.
The plate armor upon his head,
The felt skirt of that armor,
Was broad as roofing felt for four yurts;
It seemed able to crush all the ages
And cram them into one hole.
Every mortal human being,
His fly-like soul shrieking,
Would burn and crackle beneath his wrath
And be ground into dust.
Upon the brows above his eyes,
Nine vultures and black eagles
Seemed to have gathered and built their nests;
When his hellish fury surged,
The hero Seytek faced him,
The monstrous giant’s warrior son,
The infidel who would swallow the world;
They grappled and fought,
Exhausting every stratagem.
Almambet’s lion,
Külchoro, upheld by the spirit Shay,
Shouted and thrust his spear,
And with the steel-shafted spear
He shattered sixty.
Against the monstrous infidel’s son,
When the cannon fired, no flame pierced him;
When the gun fired, no bullet pierced him.
He tried the White Musket’s shot,
But the full strength of the nobles
Was steadily diminished.
His cunning was unmatched, his venom strong—
Could there be another like him in the world?
Boasting of his strength and lion-heart,
He deemed himself a hero capable
Of overturning the pillar of the universe.
Sparks flew from his dark eyes,
Fire flew from his mace,
Dust rose wherever he advanced,
And when he charged into battle,
He made dust rise among the warriors.
Raging to slaughter the people,
To wreak all the havoc he knew,
To bind and seize the common folk,
To crush rebellion forever,
Not leaving a single soul,
To pass through, slaughtering the Kyrgyz,
And roast like salt the descendants
Of Manas, blessed by Kyzır,
Eradicating them to the very root.
Leaving no root of the Kyrgyz,
He meant to carry them away as spoil,
To spread turmoil to their farthest bounds,
To wipe them out without a remnant,
The descendants of hero Manas;
This marauding swine was like
A flood sweeping across a river crossing.
The mad brute would charge,
And reach you in the blink of an eye;
His looming form was like a whole mountain,
And if he attacked a thousand men,
He seemed ready to devour them at once.
He was both flame and burning ember;
You wretch whose soul has fled,
Even hell held none like him.
At the sight of Sarybay,
Those he toppled would plunge headlong,
And those who challenged him would be consumed.
When roused, the mad brute
Seemed to be the sole
Pillar of the earth.
Clad in armor no bullet could pierce,
Prepared for the stony battlefield,
He settled grimly into his wrath;
The cast-iron head, huge as Mount Opol,
Had bound up his iron head,
His eyes blazing like embers—
Sarybay, the monstrous giant’s son,
Had no equal beneath the heavens.
He made all his weapons ready,
And strapped his sword at an angle;
His measureless form stood apart,
And if a Kyrgyz fell into his hands,
He looked as though he would never turn aside.
When roused, the mad brute
Seemed able to turn back a flood;
When he charged in fury,
Fixing his hatred upon his foe,
He seemed able to grind a mountain to dust.
When the swine surged forward,
No mountain could withstand him;
When the mighty giant charged,
No one could force him to bow,
And none who met him remained alive.
Semetey came to face him.
Sarybay raged beyond all bounds;
His bulletproof coat of mail
Was torn and shredded to pieces.
Külchoro suffered bitter hardship,
Raising cry after cry;
Almambet’s lion
Came to separate them.
Wearing the coat Aichürök had made,
And taking many Kyrgyz warriors
Who cut off heads when told to take caps,
Hero Seytek, Semetey’s son,
Advanced with his streaming banner raised;
The uproar seemed to split the earth.
He fought with consummate skill,
Thrusting his flawless spear,
And slew the finest
Of the accomplished champion’s men.
They stood face-to-face in combat,
Until both powerful arms
Of the young hero Seytek
Were paralyzed and could not be raised,
And his priceless golden head
Was wholly drenched in black blood.
For nine days he ranged in battle,
Receiving wounds all over his body.
The warriors staked all they possessed,
And, neither dead nor vanished,
Fought their way along the Ala-Too.
Against the monstrous infidel’s son,
The infidel who laid waste to the earth,
The very black angel of death,
The young hero could not prevail;
His dark eyes burned with anguish,
And he despaired of his entrusted life.
Seytek, the valiant lion,
Could no longer hold his ground,
And when he beheld the infidel’s full might,
He could not endure his dreadful form.
He grieved as he grappled with him,
And despaired of his entrusted life.
Sarybay had conceived a plan:
To pass through and slaughter them all,
To butcher their people without a survivor,
To leave not one Kyrgyz alive,
But make a massacre of them,
To cast their homeland into turmoil,
And take seventy wives and widowed sisters-in-law
Away as plunder.
Such was Sarybay’s intent,
Raging like a river in full flood,
Hardened by drinking his fill of blood,
And known throughout
The whole wide world as the monstrous giant’s son.
His strength was beyond compare,
His fury terrible, his venom potent;
Born in sand and reared on stone,
He had grown apart from decent men.
Scouring the desert, he had won his steed,
And earned the name “the monstrous giant’s son.”
Then Külchoro, upheld by the spirit Shay,
Against that roaring swine,
Charged and thrust his spear,
Tormenting and harrying
The tiny life within his breast.
He began a mighty struggle
For his true kindred people,
For the land where his cord was cut and birth-stains shed,
The land inherited from his forefathers.
He would not yield to the words
Of the monstrous infidel’s son,
The earth-scorching warrior,
The wrathful infidel
Whose arms were strong and venom fierce;
He would not surrender his hard-won land and people
To that merciless foe.
They stood locked in combat,
Fighting without rest for eighty days,
Striking and ranging back and forth,
